items.title: Meta spent $34.9B on capex last quarter, and its free cash flow went negative
items.summary: Revenue rose 26% to $64.6B, but free cash flow was −$2.1B, down from $10.6B a year ago. Meta narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to $135–145B. Zuckerberg said more than 10M people in the US and Canada have set up the Muse assistant, that it isn't global yet because it needs so much compute, and that "it's going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out."
items.why: A hyperscaler whose capex now exceeds its operating cash flow is one more reason AI infrastructure is moving to debt financing, the same pressure showing up in neocloud credit.
items.body:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms topped Wall Street revenue targets in the third quarter and forecast continued top-line growth, even as billions in legal payments for teen mental health litigation cut its operating margins in half, and massive AI investments pushed free cash flow into negative territory.
The company also said it create a Class C stock share class to help it fund the AI buildout, pay employee stock compensation, and fund acquisitions.
Investors ignored the short-term pain for the potential of a future AI payoff, cheering early signs of traction with the recently released Muse AI agent, sending Meta shares up as much as 5% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.
“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a prepared statement on Wednesday, later adding on the conference call that plans were underway to monetize Muse.
“The average revenue per American user for our existing ‘family of apps’ users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place,” Zuckerberg said.
Meta’s third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, above the $63.3 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. And the company forecast revenue for the final quarter of the year to range between $73 billion and $76 billion, compared with the $73.75 billion expected by analysts.
But Meta’s operating income of $13 billion was down 37% from the $20.5 billion it posted in the second quarter of 2025 as a result of a $10 billion settlement Meta struck with a group of attorneys general over youth safety. The terms of the settlement will see Meta pay about $18 billion to the states over the next decade, depending on cooperation from TikTok and Google’s YouTube. Without the charge, operating income would have been $22.9 billion and earnings of $7.40 a share, rather than $13 billion and $3.83.
Legal issues may continue to take a bite out of Meta’s results. Hours before Meta announced its Q3 results Wednesday, news broke that a New Mexico judge had ordered the company to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal. Meta plans to appeal.
Net income in Q3 totaled $9.9 billion, or $3.83 a share, versus $2.7 billion, or $1.05 a share in the year-ago period.
Meta is plowing unprecedented amounts of capital into AI infrastructure and services, joining companies like Alphabet , OpenAI, and Microsoft in a race to develop the most advanced AI models. To continue funding the AI effort, Meta said it would reallocate investments from its money-losing virtual reality business, Reality Labs, and that it would create a new nonvoting class C common stock.
Capital expenditures, which have tech investors on tenterhooks, clocked in at $34.9 billion, compared with $31 billion in the second quarter and $19.4 billion a year ago. Meta slightly tweaked its full year capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, from $130 billion to $145 billion.
Free cash flow, which has been a sore spot for Meta, was negative $2.1 billion, compared with $784 million in the second quarter and $10.6 billion a year ago.
The results also come a week after Meta’s Superintelligence Labs launched Muse Wonder to the public, its first frontier model , and a little over a month since Meta released its Muse virtual assistant.
Zuckerberg said that more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had already set up Muse assistant since it was released. “Because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we have not launched it globally yet,” Zuckerberg said on the earnings conference call with analysts.
Asked about Meta’s traditional playbook of monetizing new products after they reach 1 billion users, Zuckerberg said that the steep costs of running Muse and the inherent suitability of AI agents like Muse to play a role in retail transactions meant that the company would look for ways to generate revenue sooner.
“My guess is, I think that we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook,” he said.
Zuckerberg also said he was optimistic about the potential for business customers to use Muse.
Few companies are as well positioned as Meta to capitalize on the agentic AI opportunity, Zuckerberg said, though he noted that the company needed to continue making progress on compute efficiency.
“It’s going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out,” he said.
Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha research at S&P Global, wrote in a note before the results that consensus capex for 2026 had risen more than $14 billion since April to about $140 billion—almost double that of 2025. She noted that investors continue to want clarity on how that spending will translate into shareholder returns.
Overall in tech infrastructure spending, capex is expected to continue ballooning in 2026 to $790 billion, according to Otto, almost double what it was in 2025 at $404 billion. And it won’t stop there. For 2027, capex is expected to rise to $1.2 trillion, meaning companies will have spent nearly $2 trillion on the AI build-out in two years.

items.title: OpenAI reportedly nears a raise of up to $30B at a $1.25T pre-money valuation, led by UAE investors and Coatue
items.summary: Per CNBC, investors are being pitched the round as an "opportunistic" bridge to a possible IPO, and OpenAI wants signatures by the end of next week. Earlier this month OpenAI had reportedly pitched a $1.4T price, and it is separately negotiating for more compute capacity in the UAE.
items.why: A lower price on a smaller round, on the day neocloud stocks sold off, suggests even the top AI lab now faces investors who are sensitive to price.
items.body:
OpenAI is close to finalizing an up to $30 billion funding round at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, according to people familiar with the deal.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates and Coatue are leading the financing, the people said.
The financing is being positioned as a bridge ahead of a potential IPO.
OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering .
The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised.
Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO.
OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said.
Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030.
The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public."
Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported.
The company is reportedly seeking a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion in its offering. In May, Anthropic closed a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion valuation.

items.title: Neoclouds sell off: CoreWeave falls 10% to a 52-week low as Nebius takes a one-year, $3.5B loan from Citi
items.summary: Nebius's 364-day secured loan from Citi costs SOFR + 2.75% and will fund data centers and GPUs. Nebius says it still has over $40B of investment-grade contracts it can borrow against. CoreWeave closed at $55.60 after Bernstein cut its target to $51, estimating CoreWeave needs about $85B to fund its committed backlog, and some CoreWeave bonds now yield around 15%, up from 9.675% when they were issued (per Motley Fool and press reports).
items.why: The GPU build-out runs on borrowed money, so the cost of that debt is now a real limit on how fast neoclouds can add capacity, whatever Jensen Huang says about demand being "off the charts."
items.body:
Marks next step in Nebius’s strategy to fund global capacity build-out on attractive terms
Advances diversified capital structure built on a disciplined balance sheet
Increases flexibility over timing and structure of longer-term financing to fuel growth in 2027 and beyond
Amsterdam, 22 October, 2026 — Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS), the AI cloud company, today announced that it has entered into a $3.5 billion senior secured facility provided by Citi.
The facility provides access to capital at attractive rates to support Nebius’s global capacity build-out, and advances the company’s diversified and sequenced funding strategy.
It complements a funding base that includes customer prepayments and operating cash flows with other financing mechanisms.
This provides flexibility over the timing and structure of further external capital-raising as the company continues to execute on its global build-out plans.
Ophir Nave, Chief Operating Officer of Nebius, said:
“We continue to execute our funding strategy as planned, and are pleased to have secured this financing from a leading global financial institution. This is a result of our disciplined approach to managing our balance sheet to fund our portfolio of projects, and once again demonstrates our ability to choose when and how we raise capital to support our growth.
“Sequencing our financing is how we optimize our long-term cost of capital. This facility provides additional financing to support our near-term capacity build-out. We still have a range of capital sources available to us to finance the next phase of growth, including asset-backed financing based on investment-grade customer commitments of more than $40 billion of long-term contracts.”
The facility has a 364-day maturity and initially bears interest at Term SOFR plus 2.75% per annum, increasing up to a maximum of 3.50% per annum, and subject to other adjustments.
The proceeds will be used for data center development and GPU procurement, as well as for general corporate purposes.
Citi acted as mandated lead arranger, agent and security agent.
Nebius, the AI cloud company, is building the full-stack platform for developers and companies to take charge of their AI future — from data and model training to production deployment. Founded on deep in-house technological expertise and operating at scale with a rapidly expanding global footprint, Nebius serves startups and enterprises building AI products, agents, and services worldwide. Nebius is listed on Nasdaq (Nasdaq: NBIS) and headquartered in Amsterdam.

items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.summary: Elastic GPUs, sandbox growth, and the economics of the agent cloud
items.why: Modal CEO explains GPU economics and agent cloud architecture
items.body:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!
Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.
A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.
Watch the full conversation on YouTube →
A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.
Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.
There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion →
The sandbox that almost didn’t make it
Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch.
That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion →
Fast startup is an infrastructure feature
Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost.
We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture →
Modal — the AI infrastructure platform Erik founded.
Erik’s writing — his essays on infrastructure, markets, and building companies.
Modal’s Series D announcement — the company’s latest reported growth and sandbox milestones.
How Modal achieved truly serverless GPUs — the startup and scaling techniques behind elastic inference.
Modal’s resource solver — how it selects capacity across changing prices and availability.
Scaling to one million concurrent sandboxes — an engineering account of sandbox scaling.
Our first interview with Erik — the original serverless infrastructure thesis.
Our interview with Akshat Bubna — infrastructure and developer experience for agents.
The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad on GPU trading and physical settlement.

# AI's Compute Build-Out Now Has an Interest Rate Problem
*CoreWeave's bonds reportedly trade near a 15% yield, Nebius took a 364-day loan, and Meta's free cash flow went negative. The build-out runs on borrowed money now, and the price of that money sets the pace.*

Some CoreWeave bonds were issued at a 9.675% yield and now reportedly yield around 15%, per Motley Fool and press reports. The same week, Nebius signed a $3.5B senior secured facility with Citi at Term SOFR plus 2.75%, stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%. It matures in 364 days and pays for data centers and GPUs.

Then Meta reported $34.9B of capex last quarter and free cash flow of negative $2.1B, against positive $10.6B a year earlier.

I'd stop reading this week as a GPU supply story. The number setting the pace looks like the interest rate.

## The numbers flipped this quarter

For years the hyperscaler playbook was straightforward: fund the build-out from the profit machine. [Meta's Q3](https://fortune.com/2026/10/21/meta-q3-earnings-mark-zuckerberg-capex-muse/) broke that. Capex ran ahead of the cash the business produces, and free cash flow went negative $2.1B. A year ago it was $10.6B.

Revenue still rose 26% to $64.6B, so the equity story holds. The cash flow doesn't. Meta narrowed full-year 2026 capex guidance to $135B to $145B, from $130B to $145B.

Visible Alpha's Melissa Otto wrote in a note before the results that overall tech infrastructure capex is expected to reach $790B in 2026, almost double 2025's $404B, and $1.2 trillion in 2027. Her note puts the two-year spend at nearly $2 trillion. Those are estimates from Visible Alpha consensus, not reported results, and they move as guidance changes.

Zuckerberg on the call: "It's going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out." I'd read that literally. More than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up the Muse assistant, and it hasn't gone global because, in his words, "this is a compute-intensive service to run." Meta is also creating a nonvoting Class C share class to help fund the buildout.

## Neoclouds are the canary

CoreWeave's bonds are the cleanest price signal of the week. Those bonds came out at a 9.675% yield and reportedly trade near 15% now. The stock closed at a 52-week low of $55.60 after Bernstein cut its target to $51 and estimated CoreWeave needs about $85B to fund its committed backlog, per press reports.

[Nebius](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-secures-3-5-billion-financing-facility-with-citi) took the other side of that market. Its Citi facility is senior secured, matures in 364 days, and starts at SOFR plus 2.75%, stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%. Nebius calls the rates attractive and the deal part of a disciplined, sequenced funding strategy, and it says the structure gives it flexibility over when it raises longer-term capital.

A one-year maturity on data center and GPU spend means Nebius will need longer money soon. Its answer is the collateral: it says it holds more than $40B of long-term investment-grade customer contracts it can borrow against, which is how it gets to pick its timing. The next loan gets justified by a signed contract, not by a GPU sitting in a rack.

## Frontier labs feel it too

OpenAI is reportedly close to an up to $30B round at a $1.25T pre-money valuation, led by UAE investors and Coatue, per [CNBC on Oct 22](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/openai-funding-round-uae-investors.html). CNBC reports the deal is being pitched as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO, with OpenAI aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week. The same story says OpenAI had reportedly pitched a $1.4T price earlier this month.

This is the asset everyone says they have to own, and the number came down. CNBC also reports OpenAI told investors in February it is targeting roughly $600B in total compute spend by 2030, and that it is separately negotiating a commercial deal for more computing capacity in the UAE. Capital and compute are being solved in the same conversation.

I think that pattern repeats. When the money gets more expensive, the rounds get structured as bridges, and the compute deals get bundled with the check.

## What this changes for product teams

Zuckerberg said Meta will work on monetizing Muse "somewhat sooner" than its normal playbook, and gave the reason: the cost of running it. That's a financing schedule showing up as a product decision.

Erik Bernhardsson, the Modal CEO, described the demand side on [Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/modal-d), paraphrased. A typical capacity contract hands you a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period, which plots as a rectangle. Real workloads spike and fall. Buy for the peak and you pay for idle hardware. He also said he doesn't expect an imminent collapse in GPU prices, but that locking in supply at today's prices is a real risk when you build a business around it.

So the pressure runs both ways. Buyers of compute want elastic, short-duration capacity because they can't tell what next year's price is. Sellers of compute are signing fixed long contracts to finance the GPUs. Someone holds that mismatch.

For anyone shipping AI features, my read is that token prices, API quotas, and model release cadence will track financing schedules at least as much as GPU supply, so keep a fallback model you can switch to without a rewrite. Next time a vendor raises prices or throttles your quota, ask what share of this year's compute sits behind debt that matures in under two years. If they dodge it, open their most recent 10-Q and read the current portion of long-term debt and the purchase commitments line, then put the same question to them again.

# AI's Compute Build-Out Now Has an Interest Rate Problem
*CoreWeave's bonds reportedly trade near a 15% yield, Nebius took a 364-day loan, and Meta's free cash flow went negative. The build-out runs on borrowed money now, and the price of that money sets the pace.*

Some CoreWeave bonds were issued at a 9.675% yield and now reportedly yield around 15%, per Motley Fool and press reports. The same week, Nebius signed a $3.5B senior secured facility with Citi at Term SOFR plus 2.75%, stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%. It matures in 364 days and pays for data centers and GPUs.

Then Meta reported $34.9B of capex last quarter and free cash flow of negative $2.1B, against positive $10.6B a year earlier.

I'd stop reading this week as a GPU supply story. The number setting the pace looks like the interest rate.

## The numbers flipped this quarter

For years the hyperscaler playbook was straightforward: fund the build-out from the profit machine. [Meta's Q3](https://fortune.com/2026/10/21/meta-q3-earnings-mark-zuckerberg-capex-muse/) broke that. Capex ran ahead of the cash the business produces, and free cash flow went negative $2.1B. A year ago it was $10.6B.

Revenue still rose 26% to $64.6B, so the equity story holds. The cash flow doesn't. Meta narrowed full-year 2026 capex guidance to $135B to $145B, from $130B to $145B.

Visible Alpha's Melissa Otto wrote in a note before the results that overall tech infrastructure capex is expected to reach $790B in 2026, almost double 2025's $404B, and $1.2 trillion in 2027. Her note puts the two-year spend at nearly $2 trillion. Those are estimates from Visible Alpha consensus, not reported results, and they move as guidance changes.

Zuckerberg on the call: "It's going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out." I'd read that literally. More than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up the Muse assistant, and it hasn't gone global because, in his words, "this is a compute-intensive service to run." Meta is also creating a nonvoting Class C share class to help fund the buildout.

## Neoclouds are the canary

CoreWeave's bonds are the cleanest price signal of the week. Those bonds came out at a 9.675% yield and reportedly trade near 15% now. The stock closed at a 52-week low of $55.60 after Bernstein cut its target to $51 and estimated CoreWeave needs about $85B to fund its committed backlog, per press reports.

[Nebius](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-secures-3-5-billion-financing-facility-with-citi) took the other side of that market. Its Citi facility is senior secured, matures in 364 days, and starts at SOFR plus 2.75%, stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%. Nebius calls the rates attractive and the deal part of a disciplined, sequenced funding strategy, and it says the structure gives it flexibility over when it raises longer-term capital.

A one-year maturity on data center and GPU spend means Nebius will need longer money soon. Its answer is the collateral: it says it holds more than $40B of long-term investment-grade customer contracts it can borrow against, which is how it gets to pick its timing. The next loan gets justified by a signed contract, not by a GPU sitting in a rack.

## Frontier labs feel it too

OpenAI is reportedly close to an up to $30B round at a $1.25T pre-money valuation, led by SoftBank and Coatue, per [CNBC on Oct 22](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/openai-funding-round-uae-investors.html). CNBC reports the deal is being pitched as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO, with OpenAI aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week. The same story says OpenAI had reportedly pitched a $1.4T price earlier this month.

This is the asset everyone says they have to own, and the number came down. CNBC also reports OpenAI told investors in February it is targeting roughly $600B in total compute spend by 2030, and that it is separately negotiating a commercial deal for more computing capacity in the UAE. Capital and compute are being solved in the same conversation.

I think that pattern repeats. When the money gets more expensive, the rounds get structured as bridges, and the compute deals get bundled with the check.

## What this changes for product teams

Zuckerberg said Meta will work on monetizing Muse "somewhat sooner" than its normal playbook, and gave the reason: the cost of running it. That's a financing schedule showing up as a product decision.

Erik Bernhardsson, the Modal CEO, described the demand side on [Latent Space](https://www.latent.space/p/modal-d), paraphrased. A typical capacity contract hands you a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period, which plots as a rectangle. Real workloads spike and fall. Buy for the peak and you pay for idle hardware. He also said he doesn't expect an imminent collapse in GPU prices, but that locking in supply at today's prices is a real risk when you build a business around it.

So the pressure runs both ways. Buyers of compute want elastic, short-duration capacity because they can't tell what next year's price is. Sellers of compute are signing fixed long contracts to finance the GPUs. Someone holds that mismatch.

For anyone shipping AI features, my read is that token prices, API quotas, and model release cadence will track financing schedules at least as much as GPU supply, so keep a fallback model you can switch to without a rewrite. Next time a vendor raises prices or throttles your quota, ask what share of this year's compute sits behind debt that matures in under two years. If they dodge it, open their most recent 10-Q and read the current portion of long-term debt and the purchase commitments line, then put the same question to them again.
